newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel licence news eases shareholder pressure.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel licence news eases shareholder pressure.

text.p: Eurotunnel SA stock leapt on Wednesday on news that its operating licence may be extended -- news which appeared to have substantially reduced shareholder opposition to a crucial debt restructuring plan for the group.

Trading was briefly suspended in Paris after the share rose by over 20 percent. The Channel Tunnel operator's stock closed up 9.42 percent at 7.55 francs in Paris and 7.5 pence higher at 76.5 pence in London.

One group representing mainly small French shareholders said it would still resist the huge debt restructuring plan, but two others said there was no longer any reason to vote against the proposal at a meeting on July 10.

"It's a good deal as far as investor confidence is concerned because it makes the chance of a 'yes' vote (by investors for the debt plan) much higher," said analyst Richard Hannah at UBS, a veteran commentator on the company.

But he added the licence extension to at least 99 years did not have a big financial impact because it was the first few years that really counted. "If it survives 10 years, it will survive in the long term as well."
The French Finance Ministry said on Tuesday that France and Britain were ready to extend Eurotunnel SA/Plc's concession to at least 99 years from the current 65-year licence, which runs out in 2052.
Conditions included acceptance by Eurotunnel shareholders of the 70 billion francs ($12 billion) debt plan and payment of 25 percent of Eurotunnel profits from 2052.
The Eurotunnel Shareholders' Association, the more moderate of two mainly French small shareholder groups, said it would vote in favour of the plan at a shareholder meeting on July 10.

And lawyer Sophie L'Helias said in a statement that her Franklin Global Investor Services, proxy holder for various institutional investors, felt the statement by the Finance Ministry "makes it impossible for FGIS to vote against the restructuring plan that will be put to the shareholders on July 10".
On Monday, one of L'Helias's clients -- Northern Cross, which holds over three percent of Eurotunnel -- said it would vote in favour of the debt pact.

The Eurotunnel Shareholders' Association, led by Frenchman Christian Cambier, also issued a statement on Wednesday saying it hade mnade extension of the operating licence a condition of support and would now vote in favour.
But a smaller, more radical group, Adacte, said on Wednesday the licence extension did not meet one of its basic demands -- that banks cancel 40 percent of loans to Eurotunnel.

"We think the only way for Eurotunnel to be viable is that the banks abandon part of the debt," spokeswoman Emmanuelle Bobin said. Without a write-off, debt service problems would be postponed for a few years before another debt restructuring.

In any future debt deal, Adacte believes shareholders will be further diluted to a quarter of the capital from the 54.5 percent proposed in the current deal. "They will lose their voice, it will be too late," Bobin said.
Adacte has gathered proxy votes for around two million shares and expects proxies for at least 10 million for a shareholders' meeting next week which will vote on the deal.
The rival group led by Cambier said recently it represented about 25 to 30 million of the total 920 million votes.
A spokeswoman for L'Helias could not quantify the number of votes she represented.
